sections.overview: Arnoglossus scapha is a bothid flatfish known in New Zealand as witch or witch flounder, and as mahue in Māori. It occurs in the western Pacific.
sections.identification: Adults typically measure 20–30 cm long. FishBase records a maximum length of 40 cm. The thin, oval fish has both eyes on its left side, a grey or pale-brown spotted upper side, a white underside, and a strongly arched lateral line. Two other New Zealand flatfishes also have left-facing eyes, Neoachiropsetta milfordi and Lophonectes gallus; distinguish this species by its oval outline, separated pelvic fin and arched lateral line.
sections.habitat: It is recorded in the western Pacific, including New Zealand and China, across a depth range of about 20–500 m. In New Zealand it lives on soft subtidal bottoms, from shallow water to depths beyond 400 m.
sections.diet: It eats worms, crustaceans and molluscs, and may occasionally take small fish. A gut-content study found that it also feeds on benthic epifauna and pelagic organisms, unlike several co-occurring flatfishes.
sections.behavior: This is a visual feeder: unlike several New Zealand flatfishes with bottom-feeding adaptations, its prominent eyes and toothed gill rakers suit feeding above the seabed. It remains a demersal fish associated with soft-bottom habitat.
sections.reproduction: In southern New Zealand waters, spawning has been recorded from August through April, with a peak in spring. Eggs and young stages spend an extended period in the plankton before settling toward the seabed.
sections.ecology: Witch flounders are important prey for New Zealand king shags; in some studied colonies they formed most of the fish prey recorded. This links a soft-bottom predator to a specialist seabird’s feeding grounds.
sections.conservation: FishBase reports an IUCN assessment of Least Concern, made in 2019; this dated global category should not be mistaken for a current local population estimate.
